working_title: Electric or Push Trolley? What to Actually Think About Before You Buy
angle: Rather than a generic 'here are all the options' roundup, this post frames the decision as a practical checklist driven by how and where a UK club golfer actually plays, covering terrain, car boot space, frequency of play, and lithium vs lead-acid battery trade-offs, with honest notes on where the extra cost of electric is genuinely worth it and where it isn't.
research_notes:
- Electric trolleys are the dominant format in the UK in 2026; key brands are PowaKaddy, Motocaddy, Stewart Golf, and Big Max
- PowaKaddy FX3 described as the best-selling electric trolley in the UK, noted for simplicity: twist-dial speed control and widescreen display
- Motocaddy SE is positioned as the entry-level electric option; available with either a lead-acid battery or lithium battery — lead-acid is cheaper but heavier, lithium doesn't need to be removed for charging
- Electric trolley prices in 2026 run from roughly £429–£499 at entry level up to around £1,200+ for GPS flagship models (e.g. PowaKaddy CT12 GPS)
- Push trolleys start from around £100; brands include Big Max, Sun Mountain, Motocaddy, PowaKaddy, MacGregor, Wishbone, Benross
- Benross Pro Compact noted as popular and well-engineered at under £150 (steel frame, ergonomic handles, umbrella holder included)
- Key practical trade-offs: electric trolleys are heavier and bulkier to fold and store; push trolleys are lighter, easier to transport, no charging required
- Electric trolleys genuinely earn their cost on hilly courses; on flat parkland the benefit is real but less dramatic
- Advanced electric features in 2026 include built-in GPS (up to 40,000 preloaded courses on some models), remote control, and 'follow' modes where trolley tracks the golfer autonomously
- Follow-mode trolleys (e.g. Stewart Golf Q Follow) require a charged remote at all times — worth flagging as a maintenance consideration
- Lithium batteries on better electric models don't need to be removed for charging — a meaningful convenience point for UK golfers storing trolleys in garages
- Push trolleys better suited to: flat courses, golfers who value the exercise element, smaller car boots, and those who play fewer than 2–3 times per week
- Electric trolleys better suited to: hilly or undulating courses, golfers playing 3+ times per week, anyone with back or shoulder concerns
- Maintenance note for electric: clean wheels after every use (mud, sand, grass), keep battery charged per manufacturer guidance
must_avoid:
- Do not fabricate specific prices beyond the ranges found in research (push from ~£100, electric entry ~£429–£499, top-end ~£1,200+); describe mid-range figures in general terms if not confirmed
- No invented quotes from pros, reviewers, or brand representatives
- No health or medical advice beyond generic practical guidance (e.g. 'takes strain off your shoulders on hilly courses' is fine; specific injury claims are not)
- No affiliate links for any trolley brand unless they appear in /src/content/approved-partners.md
- No financial advice framing (e.g. do not say 'the electric is worth the investment for your budget'); describe costs factually only
- No em dashes anywhere in the post
- No first-person anecdotes implying the site owner has used or owns any specific trolley model
